results.tides: Ocean tides happen because the Moon's gravity pulls harder on the side of Earth closest to it than on the side farther away, stretching the oceans into two bulges — one facing the Moon, one on the opposite side. As Earth rotates through these bulges roughly every 24 hours, most coastlines experience two high tides and two low tides a day. The Sun adds a weaker version of the same effect, so tides are extra strong (spring tides) when the Sun and Moon align, and weaker (neap tides) when they're at right angles.
results.autumn_leaves: Leaves change color in autumn because shorter days and cooler temperatures cause trees to stop producing chlorophyll, the green pigment that dominates leaves during the growing season and masks other pigments. As chlorophyll breaks down, yellow and orange pigments (carotenoids) that were present all along become visible, while some trees also produce new red and purple pigments (anthocyanins) in response to the changing conditions. This process is part of the tree sealing off and shedding its leaves before winter, when cold weather would make photosynthesis inefficient anyway.
results.bread_rising: Yeast is a living microorganism that feeds on sugars in the dough and, through fermentation, produces carbon dioxide gas and a bit of alcohol as byproducts. The gluten network formed by kneading the flour and water traps these CO2 bubbles rather than letting them escape, so the dough expands like a stretchy balloon. As more gas is produced over time, the dough continues to rise until it's baked, at which point the heat sets the structure permanently.
